story: The Bungle Bungle Range covers about 45,000 hectares of the park and is the most outstanding example of cone karst in sandstone anywhere in the world. The sandstone was laid down about 360 million years ago; over the past 20 million years creeks, rivers and weathering have carved it into domes, chasms and gorges. The domes' bands come from life: grey layers are coated with cyanobacteria where moisture collects in the rock, and orange layers are oxidised iron compounds that dried out too quickly for the cyanobacteria to grow.

The range has two distinct ends. In the north, open woodland and spinifex give way to hidden chasms and towering cliffs lined with Livistona palms, at Echidna Chasm, Mini Palms Gorge and Homestead Valley. In the south stand the iconic beehive domes, Cathedral Gorge's great red amphitheatre and Piccaninny Creek winding towards the Ord River. More than 600 plant species have been recorded, including 13 kinds of spinifex, more than anywhere else in Australia, and sheltered gorges hold the most southerly patches of rainforest in the East Kimberley. Over 149 bird species live here, among them the white-quilled rock pigeon, and at least one endemic skink.

The Gija and Jaru people are the Traditional Owners of Purnululu. Aboriginal people maintain a strong connection to this ancient landscape, expressed through story, song, art and visits, and continue to use resources that have sustained them for thousands of years. They ask visitors to walk only on marked trails, leave everything as they find it and never climb on the rock structures, which are fragile and break easily. A short trail at Stonehenge introduces the traditional Aboriginal uses of trees, shrubs and grasses.

Purnululu was declared a national park in 1987 and lies between the Purnululu Conservation Reserve and the Ord River Regeneration Reserve. In 2003 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List for its natural beauty and its outstanding geological value. It is run by the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), whose new visitor centre, where every visitor registers, uses virtual reality to take visitors into its gorges.
howItWorks: Purnululu is one of Western Australia's national parks managed by DBCA's Parks and Wildlife Service, and one of more than 30 WA parks that charge an entry fee. The standard fee is per vehicle and covers one day's entry to one or more parks; a WA park pass, from a five-day Holiday Pass to an Annual All Parks Pass, covers entry to every WA park for its duration but not camping. Register and pay park fees at the Purnululu Visitor Centre before driving further into the park. Campers pay entry only for the first day.

The park is open only in the dry season, generally from April or May to late November, weather permitting, and closes for the wet. The only way in is the 53-kilometre Spring Creek Track from the Great Northern Highway, which takes 1.5 to 3 hours in a high-clearance four-wheel drive; single-axle off-road trailers are allowed, dual-axle trailers are not, and there is no fuel in the park. Walardi and Kurrajong campgrounds must be booked through Park Stay WA, up to 180 days ahead, for the May–September season; you choose from the sites vacant when you arrive. Two privately run glamping camps stand along Bellburn Creek.

Rules are strict in this fragile place. No campfires at any time, no generators at the campgrounds, no dogs or other pets, no firearms and no fishing. Purnululu is drone-free: unauthorised drones are prohibited. The Piccaninny Gorge Trek, beyond the normal walk trail classes and only for very experienced hikers, must be booked online for the 2026 season. Helicopters fly over the park all day; do not wave at them unless you need help.

sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-cathedral-gorge: A vast natural amphitheatre of red rock hidden among the striped domes, reached on a moderately difficult two-kilometre return walk from the Piccaninny car park.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-the-domes: A 1.4-kilometre walk among the famous beehive domes of the southern range, for those who want the landscape without a long hike.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-piccaninny-creek: The Creek Lookout Trail follows the eroded creek bed to views of the creek winding south towards the Ord River; the multi-day Piccaninny Gorge Trek must be booked.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-the-window: A naturally formed sandstone window among the beehive domes, at the end of a six-kilometre return trail.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-echidna-chasm: A two-kilometre return walk into a chasm with walls up to 200 metres high and barely a metre apart in places, lined with prehistoric Livistona palms.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-mini-palms-gorge: A challenging 4.4-kilometre return trail over boulders and narrow edges to platforms above an amphitheatre filled with small palms.
sightNotes.poi-au-purnululu-kungkalanayi-lookout: A short, steep climb to a ridge with 360-degree views of the western escarpment of the Bungle Bungle Range; good at sunrise and sunset.

entrances: The Spring Creek Track, 53 kilometres of unsealed, corrugated road with creek crossings from the Great Northern Highway to the visitor centre; high-clearance four-wheel drive only
Scenic light-plane and helicopter flights over the range from the Bellburn airstrip
planYourVisit.reservations: Book Walardi or Kurrajong campground through Park Stay WA, up to 180 days ahead; the glamping camps on Bellburn Creek are booked through the Kununurra Visitor Centre. Book the Piccaninny Gorge Trek online. Check DBCA Park Alerts and Main Roads WA for the opening date and track conditions before you go.
permits: Park entry fee or a valid WA park pass, paid at the visitor centre
A booking for the Piccaninny Gorge Trek, which exceeds the standard walk trail classes
camping: Walardi campground, 12 kilometres south of the visitor centre and closest to the Domes and Cathedral Gorge: 37 unpowered sites, no-flush toilets
Kurrajong campground, towards the north of the park, 7 kilometres from the visitor centre
No campfires and no generators; untreated bore water must be treated before drinking; carry all rubbish out
lodging: Two privately run glamping camps on Bellburn Creek, booked in advance
seasonalClosures: The park closes for the wet season, generally from late November to April or May — check DBCA Park Alerts before you go

chronology.text: The sandstone of the Bungle Bungle Range is deposited.
Purnululu is inscribed on the World Heritage List for its natural beauty and geology.
Online booking is required for the Piccaninny Gorge Trek for the season.

safety: Temperatures can exceed 40°C, and radiant heat off the rock can push them over 50°C. Walk in the cooler parts of the day, wear a hat and long sleeves, and drink a litre of water per hour of walking.

There is no phone service on the way in or in most of the park, only intermittent Optus coverage at the visitor centre and campgrounds. Carry a personal locator beacon or satellite phone; in an emergency use UHF channel 1 duplex (north) or 4 duplex (south).
If you break down on the Spring Creek Track, stay with your vehicle, raise the bonnet and wait for the next vehicle.
Stay on marked trails and do not climb on the domes: the rock is fragile and breaks easily.
Treat bore water before drinking it, and watch for livestock and wildlife on the track.
regulations: Pay park entry at the visitor centre or carry a valid WA park pass.
Purnululu is a drone-free area; unauthorised drone use is prohibited.
No campfires at any time, and no generators at the campgrounds.
Only high-clearance four-wheel drives and single-axle trailers on the Spring Creek Track; dual-axle trailers are not permitted.

weather: Purnululu has the Kimberley's wet and dry seasons. The park opens in the dry, from about April or May to late November, when days are clear; the tourist season for campground bookings runs from May to September. Even in the dry, temperatures can exceed 40°C during the day, and radiant heat off the rock can push it above 50°C, so walk in the cooler parts of the day and drink a litre of water per hour of walking. In the wet season, roughly December to March, heavy rain closes the Spring Creek Track and the park.
directions: Purnululu is 304 kilometres by road from Kununurra and 160 kilometres from Halls Creek, off the Great Northern Highway. The last 53 kilometres, the Spring Creek Track, is unsealed, rocky, sandy and corrugated, with creek crossings that may be dry only late in the season; it takes 1.5 to 3 hours, the speed limit is 50 km/h, and only high-clearance four-wheel drives and single-axle off-road trailers may use it. Carry enough fuel for at least 300 kilometres, spare tyres and recovery gear, and lower tyre pressures. The northern and southern ends of the range are 47 kilometres apart, an 80-minute drive.
